items.title: Spin dynamics and ortho–para conversion in $H_{2}O$ during the phase transition from gas to solid in external magnetic fields
items.summary: The spin dynamics of water ice in the presence of external magnetic fields are investigated. The employedmodel is based on the approach introduced by Buntkowsky et al. (2008), which considers two nearest-neighbor water molecules and yields a four-spin system, as the abundant oxygen isotope has zero nuclear spin.The model is extended to include coupling to external magnetic fields, allowing us to analyze the interplaybetween magnetic dipole–dipole interactions and magnetic field coupling. Two types of configurations areexamined: (i) static, homogeneous fields, corresponding to a time-independent interaction, and (ii) spatiallyvarying sinusoidal fields in relative motion with the molecules, leading to a time-dependent interaction.All computations are performed within the density operator formalism. The ortho/para populations and thetotal spin projections are evaluated during the first tens of milliseconds following the gas-to-solid phasetransition. For static homogeneous fields, we show that increasing field strength suppresses dipolar-induceddepolarization. Assuming that all molecules are initially in the para state, we show that static homogeneousfields can drive the ortho population up to approximately 50%, whereas suitably chosen sinusoidal-fieldconfigurations can increase it beyond 90%. These results are relevant for schemes aiming to preserve ormanipulate nuclear-spin polarization during deposition.

items.title: Spin-adapted neural network wavefunctions in real space
items.summary: Spin plays a fundamental role in understanding electronic structure, yet many real-space wavefunction methods fail to adequately consider it. We introduce the Spin-Adapted Antisymmetrization Method (SAAM), a general procedure that enforces exact total spin symmetry for antisymmetric many-electron wavefunctions in real space. In the context of neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo (NNQMC), SAAM leverages the expressiveness of deep neural networks to capture electron correlation while enforcing exact spin adaptation via group representation theory. This framework provides a principled route to embed physical priors into otherwise black-box neural network wavefunctions, yielding a compact representation of correlated system with neural network orbitals. Compared with existing treatments of spin in NNQMC, SAAM is more accurate and efficient, achieving exact spin purity without any additional tunable hyperparameters. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply SAAM to study the spin ladder of iron-sulfur clusters, a long-standing challenge for many-body methods due to their dense spectrum of nearly degenerate spin states. Our results reveal accurate resolution of low-lying spin states and spin gaps in [Fe$_2$S$_2$] and [Fe$_4$S$_4$] clusters, offering new insights into their electronic structures. In sum, these findings establish SAAM as a robust, hyperparameter-free standard for spin-adapted NNQMC, particularly for strongly correlated systems.

items.title: Hook Immanantal Inequalities for Totally Nonnegative Matrices
items.summary: Given a weakly decreasing positive integer sequence $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\dotsc,\lambda_\ell)$ summing to $n$, let $\chi^\lambda$ denote the irreducible character of the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$ indexed by $\lambda$. This representation has dimension $\chi^\lambda(e)$, where $e$ is the identity element of $\mathfrak{S}_n$. Let $\mathrm{Imm}_{\chi^\lambda}$ denote the corresponding irreducible character immanant, the function on $n \times n$ matrices $A = (a_{i,j})$ defined by$$\mathrm{Imm}_{\chi^\lambda}(A) := \negthickspace \sum_{w \in \mathfrak{S}_n} \negthickspace \chi^\lambda(w) \hspace{.5mm} a_{1,w_1} \cdots a_{n,w_n}.$$Merris conjectured [Linear Multilinear Algebra 14 (1983) pp. 21--35] and Heyfron proved [Linear Multilinear Algebra 24 (1988) pp. 65--78] that irreducible character immanants indexed by "hook" sequences $(k, 1, \dotsc, 1)$ satisfy the inequalities$$\frac{\mathrm{Imm}_{\chi^n}(A)}{\chi^{n}(e)}\geq \frac{\mathrm{Imm}_{\chi^{n-1,1}}(A)}{\chi^{n-1,1}(e)}\geq \frac{\mathrm{Imm}_{\chi^{ n-2,1,1}}(A)}{\chi^{n-2,1,1}(e)}\geq \cdots \geq \frac{\mathrm{Imm}_{\chi^{1,\dotsc,1}}(A)}{\chi^{1,\dotsc,1}(e)},$$whenever $A$ is an $n \times n$ Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix. We prove that the same inequalities hold whenever $A$ is an $n \times n$ totally nonnegative matrix.
items.author: Mark A. Skandera

items.title: Floquet-ADAPT-VQE: A Quantum Algorithm to Simulate Non-Equilibrium Physics in Periodically Driven Systems
items.summary: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit many fascinating phenomena absent in equilibrium systems, but their simulation is more challenging than that of static systems. Consequently, quantum simulation of these systems offers greater opportunity for achieving quantum advantage. To build the foundation for simulating time-periodic Hamiltonians, we utilize the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism to transform the Hamiltonian into a time-independent form and provide its Pauli decomposition. Within this formalism, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, that produces three key quantities that govern periodically driven quantum dynamics: the quasienergy, the associated Floquet eigenstates, and expectation values of observables with respect to these eigenstates. The latter is achieved by applying a fixed-depth quantum circuit to an initial Floquet eigenstate—an efficient construction made possible by the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism. We also identify a suitable auxiliary initial state whose squared Floquet energy is independent of the number of auxiliary qubits as well as the driving frequency, which leads to better convergence with fewer ADAPT iterations. We demonstrate our algorithm by performing numerical simulations on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field. We also explore potential applications of our algorithm for studying various non-equilibrium phenomena in periodically driven systems.
items.author: Abhishek Kumar, Karunya Shirali, Nicholas J. Mayhall, Sophia E. Economou et al.

items.title: Noise-Induced Thermalization in Quantum Systems
items.summary: Abstract In the current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum era, noise is widely regarded as the primary obstacle to achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, certain stages of the quantum computing pipeline can, in fact, benefit from this noise. In this work, we exploit the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis to show that O(1) number of noise occurrences can accelerate a fundamental task in quantum computing -- the preparation of Gibbs states. We demonstrate this behavior using classical simulations with Haar-random and phase-flip noise, respectively, on a spin-1/2 chain with a local Hamiltonian. Our non-integrable model sees ~3.5x faster thermalization in the presence of noise, while our integrable model reaches a state that lies between a generalized Gibbs state and a Gibbs state due to noise. Since certifying a local Gibbs state is relatively easy on a quantum computer, our approach provides a new practical solution to a key problem in quantum computing. More broadly, these results establish a new paradigm in which noise can be harnessed on quantum computers, enabling practical advantages before the years of fault-tolerance.
items.author: Sameer Dambal, Yu Zhang, Eric Bittner, Pavan Hosur

items.title: Generating persistent-current superpositions in Bose-Einstein condensates using dynamic optical potentials
items.summary: Precise and flexible manipulation of the motional state of ultracold atoms is a fundamental enabling technology for diverse applications such as quantum sensing and quantum computation. In this paper we propose a general, simple and highly efficient method to engineer the motional state of a Bose-Einstein condensate with time-dependent optical fields, which can be realized experimentally with existing light sculpting techniques. We demonstrate numerically how to engineer superpositions of persistent currents in a toroidal trap, achieving very high fidelity. We also study in detail the stability of the state over time, and we present an analytical two-state model that approximates well the evolution of the state in presence of self-interactions.
items.author: Renzo Testa, Donatella Cassettari

items.title: Optimal Accelerated Life Testing Sampling Plan Design With Piecewise Linear Function Based Modeling of Lifetime Characteristics
items.summary: ABSTRACT Researchers have widely used accelerated life tests to determine an optimal inspection plan for lot acceptance. All such plans are proposed by assuming a known relationship between the lifetime characteristic(s) and the accelerating stress factor(s) under a parametric framework of the product lifetime distribution. As the true relationship is rarely known in practical scenarios, the assumption itself may produce biased estimates that may lead to an inefficient sampling plan. To this endeavor, an optimal accelerating life test plan is designed under a Type‐I censoring scheme with a generalized link structure similar to a spline regression, to capture the nonlinear relationship between the lifetime characteristics and the stress levels. Product lifetime is assumed to follow Weibull distribution with non‐identical scale and shape parameters linked with the stress factor through a piecewise linear function. The elements of the Fisher information matrix are computed in detail to formulate the acceptability criterion for the conforming lots. The decision variables of the sampling plan including sample size, stress factors, and others are determined using a constrained aggregated cost minimization approach and variance minimization approach. A simulated case study demonstrates that the nonlinear link‐based piecewise linear approximation model outperforms the linear link‐based model.
items.author: Sandip Barui, Shovan Chowdhury

items.title: Charge Transfer with a Spin. I: A Variational Constrained-CASSCF Framework for Investigating Charge Transfer in the Presence of Spin–Orbit Coupling
items.summary: Abstract Charge transfer in open-shell molecular systems can involve a delicate interplay between charge localization, orbital relaxation, and spin–orbit coupling (SOC), particularly near ground-excited state crossings. Here, we introduce a very inexpensive variational framework for treating these effects in odd-electron systems by extending the electron/hole-transfer Dynamically weighted State-Averaged Constrained CASSCF (eDSC/hDSC) method to include SOC. Our method incorporates the SOC Hamiltonian directly into the variational orbital optimization through complex-valued spinor orbitals, allowing orbital and spin degrees of freedom to relax self-consistently while preserving the time-reversal symmetry of doublet states. The method achieves smooth potential energy surfaces and rapid self-consistent field (SCF) convergence; moreover, from physically small to artificially large SOC strengths, the calculation can be converged to very tight thresholds across the whole potential energy surface. While the results presented here are for systems with two charge centers, as shown in the appendix, the theory is quite general and can be adapted to either a system of N charge centers or a metal-molecule surface with a continuum of states, so that charge transport (and not just charge transfer) can also be studied. The approach therefore provides a route toward ab initio studies of spin-dependent charge transfer and charge transport in molecular systems with nontrivial spin degrees of freedom.
items.source: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
items.author: Alok Kumar, Zhen Tao, Joseph Eli Subotnik, Tian Qiu

items.title: Tracing the film structure of an organic semiconductor with photoemission orbital tomography
items.summary: Photoemission orbital tomography (POT) is a powerful tool for investigating the orbitals and electronic band structure of oriented layers of organic molecules. In many cases, POT allows conclusions to be drawn regarding the geometric structure, but so far it has been mainly applied to (sub)monolayers and rarely to bilayers, raising the question of whether POT can also provide structure information for thicker films. Here, we use POT to analyze the band dispersion in up to eight layers of $α$-sexithiophene (6T) adsorbed on Cu(110)-p($2\times1$)O. This linear oligomer turns out to be a textbook example that exemplifies the concepts of intra- and intermolecular band dispersion in molecules. Moreover, the rich band and orbital structure information available from POT for this system enables us to trace subtle changes in the crystal structure as a function of layer thickness. Specifically, we find that the periodicity of an intermolecular band changes with film thickness, revealing an increase of the intralayer distance between the molecules with the number of layers. At the same time, the momentum distribution of photoemission from the highest occupied molecular orbital of 6T discloses a decrease of the molecular tilt angle. Following the evolution of tilt angle and lattice constant with layer thickness, we observe -- purely based on electronic structure data -- that the surface-templated monolayer structure relaxes into the structure of bulk 6T crystals. The experimental findings agree well with the results of density functional theory calculations.
items.author: Monja Stettner, Siegfried Kaidisch, A. V. Matetskiy, Eric Fackelman et al.

items.title: Engineering quantum phases in two dimensions via vacancy-induced electronic reconstruction
items.summary: Topological phases of matter are commonly understood as emerging from crystalline symmetry and intrinsic spin-orbit coupling or, less frequently, from disorder-driven electronic renormalization. In realistic materials, however, structural defects naturally combine both ingredients. Here, we propose a universal mechanism by which atomic vacancies drive a topological phase transitions in two-dimensional semiconductors through electronic reconstruction. We show that vacancies generate locally ordered dangling-bond states governed by well-defined hopping and spin-orbit interactions, while their spatial distribution and mutual coupling introduce long-range disorder. As vacancy concentration increases, the hybridization of these defect states forms an emergent electronic subspace that undergoes a topological transition. By combining large-scale density functional theory calculations with an interpretable orbital based Hamiltonian, we find that this vacancy-induced electronic reconstruction can stabilize quantum spin Hall, quantum anomalous Hall, and Weyl semimetal phases. Our results indicate vacancies not as detrimental perturbations, but as active design elements capable of transforming trivial insulators into topological quantum matter, providing realistic routes for defect-engineered topological devices. Topological phases of matter typically arise from crystalline symmetry and spin–orbit coupling, but structural defects in materials can also play a crucial role. Here, the authors demonstrate that atomic vacancies in two-dimensional semiconductors can induce topological phase transitions, suggesting vacancies as transformative elements for designing defect-engineered topological devices.
items.author: Emmanuel V. C. Lopes, F. Crasto de Lima, Caio Lewenkopf, A. Fazzio

items.title: Physics-aware neural networks enable robust and full atomic structure determination via low-dose atomic electron tomography
items.summary: Atomic electron tomography (AET) determines the three-dimensional (3D) coordinates and chemical identities of individual atoms from a series of scanning transmission electron microscopy images taken at different tilt angles. However, under dose-limited conditions, particularly at electron doses lower than those typically used for standard AET of beam-robust inorganic nanoparticles, the reduced signal-to-noise ratio forces a trade-off among accuracy, robustness, and throughput. Here, we introduce a physics-aware, two-stage neural network (PANN) that incorporates physical constraints throughout its workflow to achieve accurate AET under low-dose imaging. First, a global-local 3D ResUNet refines the initial reconstruction and corrects geometric distortions in the volume. Second, the local density around each identified atom is encoded using 3D Zernike moments. These feature descriptors, along with the atomic coordinates, are then processed by a graph-attention Transformer to classify the elemental species. We benchmark the PANN workflow using a dataset of 42,588 simulated reconstructed volumes, covering diverse noise models, material morphologies, and dose settings. Under reduced-dose conditions relative to conventional AET of beam-robust inorganic nanoparticles, PANN significantly improves performance, reducing the atomic coordinate error and leading to an increase in the atomic recovery rate. The framework’s performance on retrospectively reduced-dose experimental AET data of metallic nanoparticles demonstrates robust post-processing capability within this material class. Together with multi-slice simulation-based demonstrations on selected inorganic crystalline dose-sensitive systems, including halide perovskites, zeolites, and quantum dots, these results suggest a rout
items.author: Yao Zhang, Lanyi Cao, Zhen Sun, Jihan Zhou

items.title: What does quantum parameter estimation estimate? A no-go result for true quantity values
items.summary: We examine the conditions under which quantum parameter estimation is compatible with the concept of a ``true'' quantity value: a unique value of the estimated quantity that exists prior to and independently of measurement. While quantum parameter estimation typically assumes that the quantity to be estimated is a parameter, we argue that this assumption can be lifted, opening the way to a more general formulation of estimation that may apply even in situations where the quantity to be estimated is no longer a parameter, but instead a quantum variable susceptible to quantum fluctuations. We identify three assumptions that characterize the way estimation is often presented in the quantum metrology literature, namely, as a procedure for inferring an unknown ``true value", which is assumed to be unique and to exist prior to and independently of measurement. Using our more general framework, we prove a no-go theorem showing that the preceding assumptions are jointly incompatible with two further assumptions: the completeness of the quantum state (no `hidden variables'), and the presence of entanglement between the probe systems and the system under measurement. We note that the presence of such entanglement is a generic prediction of standard quantum theory. Consequently, if one is not willing to accept hidden variables, nor willing to modify standard quantum theory by introducing a new physical mechanism that destroys entanglement at some scale or regime, then a realist account of estimation is ultimately impossible.
items.author: Jacques L. Pienaar, Eran Tal, Asya Ciftci

items.title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
items.summary: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode m
items.author: Ouns El Harzli, Jelle Bor, Linde Wester, Leonid Zhukov et al.

items.title: Mixed State Deep Thermalization under Generic Quantum Errors
items.summary: Pure-state deep thermalization predicts that, after sufficient scrambling, projected ensembles approach universal distributions that contain information beyond the reduced density matrix. In realistic quantum systems, however, noise is unavoidable and the projected states are generally mixed. Whether mixed-state deep thermalization admits an analogous universal limiting distribution has remained unclear. Here we answer this question for quantum dynamics containing local quantum channels, i.e., errors. We show that the late-time mixed-state projected ensemble is completely determined by the normalized Choi state of the error channel and is universal, independent of the microscopic details of the underlying unitary dynamics. We establish this result analytically for dual-unitary circuits, global Haar-random dynamics, and local Haar-random circuits at large local dimension, and verify it numerically in qubit circuits and kicked Ising dynamics. In a solvable setting, we further find exponentially fast convergence to the limiting ensemble. Our results extend deep thermalization to noisy quantum dynamics and establish a direct correspondence between quantum errors and universal random mixed-state ensembles.
items.author: Xie-Hang Yu, Pavel Kos

items.title: Size-independent Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities for Quantum Gibbs Samplers
items.summary: We propose a new method for proving $L^2$ and modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities with constants independent of system size for quantum Gibbs samplers whose Lindblad generators satisfy Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) detailed balance. We first establish the $L^2$ logarithmic Sobolev inequality by transporting it along a temperature-dependent path from the infinite-temperature product state to the target Gibbs state while maintaining a size-independent decay rate for the sandwiched Rényi-2 divergence. A tensor-power argument, combined with the quantum asymptotic equipartition property, then transfers this decay bound to relative entropy, yielding the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. This approach provides a general framework for proving size-independent logarithmic Sobolev inequalities for quantum Gibbs samplers. We apply it to two regimes: one-dimensional quantum spin chains at every finite temperature, and finite-range quantum spin systems at sufficiently high temperature in any fixed dimension.
items.author: Hongrui Chen, Zhiyan Ding, Jianfeng Lu

items.title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation
items.summary: Tensor-network simulation of quantum circuits depends on contraction orders with low computational cost and small intermediate tensors, found without excessive planning time. We present ArcTN, a contraction-order optimization framework with two search presets. Light keeps planning overhead low, and Heavy spends more effort on refinement. Both combine randomized-greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering with stage-specific stopping rules. ArcTN also provides Fixed and Dynamic slicing to meet tensor-size limits and executes the returned orders. On the 30 QC32 quantum-circuit networks completed by all eight compared configurations, Light reduces FLOPs by 61.32% and plans 1.62$\times$ faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA-ES, and Heavy reduces FLOPs by 43.83% and plans 7.21$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ/Optuna. Heavy also needs 11.85% fewer FLOPs than OMECO TreeSA-8 and plans 1.33$\times$ faster. Dynamic slicing meets the size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar-output networks and reduces total sliced FLOPs by 31.99% relative to Fixed slicing, at the cost of longer planning. With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. On 672 networks built from 320 MQT Bench circuits, Heavy obtains the lowest geometric-mean FLOPs on the 142 large networks while planning 3.1$\times$ and 31$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ and Hyper128.
items.author: Zhengyi Liu, Li Liu, Songtao Liu, Xianglong Liu et al.

items.title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
items.summary: Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.
items.author: Brian Coyle, Jonathan H. Fetherolf, Antonio Márquez Romero, Stefano Scali et al.

items.title: One-shot entanglement generation and distillation via Petz recovery and binary hypothesis testing
items.summary: How much entanglement can two distant laboratories share when their connection is noisy? We relate this question to deciding which of two quantum hypotheses is present. Our one-shot bounds apply to entanglement generation over a quantum channel and to one-way entanglement distillation from a shared state. We use Cheng's trace inequality to bound the infidelity of a Petz decoder in terms of a binary hypothesis testing cost. Applying the inequality before averaging over codes reduces the error analysis to computing a second moment of random subspaces. The proof covers every integer target dimension and treats rank-deficient states explicitly. A corollary expresses the achievable entanglement through hypothesis-testing coherent information, with a single logarithmic error slack and exact integer rounding. We also prove an error-preserving conversion from entanglement generation codes to entanglement transmission codes: the target dimension decreases by only a constant factor at fixed error, and the decoder is the original decoder followed by local processing. Consequently, for both entanglement generation and entanglement transmission, arbitrary pure reference-input states yield the same coherent-information rate, second-order Gaussian correction at the original error tolerance, and explicit achievable logarithmic remainder. For commuting testing hypotheses, the logarithmic remainder improves to a constant. These results give a direct route from binary distinguishability to explicit recovery guarantees and finite-resource quantum communication rates.
items.author: Matthew Can, Mark M. Wilde

items.title: The Impact of Markovian Errors on Random Circuits
items.summary: Randomized benchmarking (RB) returns a single decay parameter or gate error rate, but when the noise is gate-dependent that parameter is notoriously difficult to interpret. We study RB and related random-circuit benchmarks under small gate-local Markovian noise by factorizing each noisy gate into its ideal action followed by the exponential of a small error generator and then perturbing the RB $\mathscr{L}$ matrix, which models the RB decay. For any low-error gate set that satisfies the requirements of RB (it is a sequence-asymptotic unitary 2-design), we show that Pauli-stochastic error rates contribute linearly to the RB decay parameter, while Hamiltonian error rates contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form. Pauli-correlation and active generators are absent from the linear term and enter only at higher order. For the single-qubit native gate set $\{X_{π/2},Y_{π/2}\}$ we derive this quadratic form explicitly in terms of three first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) coordinates: the two intrinsic over-rotations and one relational axis-tilt error. The resulting formula explains the dependence of DRB on the sampling distribution and the compilation dependence of CRB. These results turn RB decay rates into interpretable functions of experimentally meaningful elementary error rates.
items.author: Anthony M. Polloreno, Timothy Proctor, Robin Blume-Kohout

items.title: Nanopillar metasurfaces uniting high optical reflectivity with ultracoherent nanomechanics
items.summary: Mechanically compliant mirrors are key components in cavity optomechanics. However, the requirements to achieve the best optical and mechanical performance are usually in direct competition. A high reflectivity for tightly focused beams entails thick reflectors, whereas ultracoherent flexural nanomechanics necessitates thin membranes. We eliminate this trade-off by introducing high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurfaces on top of a thin membrane. We pattern a 50 micrometer-diameter array of nanopillars to form a photonic crystal. The flat band behavior of guided resonances in the photonic crystal enables a reflectivity of 99.82(1)% for a tightly focused beam of 7 micrometer waist. The combination of two guided resonances creates a 100 nanometer-wide high-reflectivity band around 1550 nanometer. Simultaneously, the nanopillar patterning realizes a density-modulated phononic crystal that isolates an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode with a $Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}$Hz. The demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces enable lightweight mirrors for room-temperature quantum optomechanics and for use as levitated mirrors or lightsails.
items.author: Alexander Jung, Anastasiia Ciers, Hannes Pfeifer, Albert Hansson et al.

items.title: ConQEC: Concolic Testing for Quantum Error-Correcting Code Implementations
items.summary: Quantum error-correcting code (QECC) implementations are hybrid software-control systems: measured syndromes drive decoder dispatch, recovery actions, and logical checks. Existing QECC verification techniques can prove formal obligations, and general quantum testing can expose final failures, but developers still lack a scalable testing workflow that generates concrete faults and explains where a QECC repair path first diverges. This paper presents ConQEC, to our knowledge the first concolic testing framework for QECC implementations. By combining concrete (Pauli) fault replay with symbolic repair-path constraints, ConQEC generates tests that expose not only final logical failures but also fault--syndrome--decoder--recovery (FSDR) diagnostics: the injected fault, observed syndrome, decoder decision, recovery action, oracle result, and earliest divergent stage. Its symbolic encoding of Pauli faults, syndrome predicates, decoder and recovery relations, and oracle checks enables this diagnostic workflow to scale beyond exponentially increasing amplitude-level quantum-state reasoning. We implemented ConQEC and evaluated it on generated source-level QECC families and public QECC artifacts with up to thousands of qubits. ConQEC detects the seeded bug in every experimental case and reports a replay-valid, fault-localizing FSDR witness for each.
items.author: Zihao Li, Ji Guan, Mingsheng Ying

items.title: Nonlinear quantum noise polarization in macroscopic nonlinear QED
items.summary: We construct a quantum theory of light in nonlinearly responding materials with dispersion and absorption and, in particular, show the emergence of non-Gaussian noise associated with nonlinear absorption processes. Our theory is based on a path-integral formulation of the microscopic Huttner-Barnett model including cubic matter self-interaction required for $χ^{(2)}$ nonlinear processes. We show that the noise polarization emerges naturally from a decoupling of the stochastic weights of the bath response which, in case of cubic self-interactions, leads to a decoupling via Airy functions. As the theory is, by construction, consistent with the nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation theorem, it constitutes a viable quantum theory of light in nonlinear media.
items.author: Arman Kashef, Stefan Scheel, Marco Ornigotti

items.title: Predictive electronic feedback control for narrow-linewidth lasers
items.summary: Narrow-linewidth lasers are essential for various key atom-laser interaction processes and optical setups in quantum coherent control, quantum precision measurement, and quantum information science. The Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) technique is the standard method for the frequency-stabilization of narrow-linewidth lasers, but the inherent time delay in its feedback loop inevitably induces excessive phase noise, commonly known as servo bumps. Previous solutions primarily rely on additional optical components outside the electronic feedback control loop. Here, we propose and implement a generic method based on the Smith predictor to address the time-delay issue entirely within the electronic part of the PDH feedback control loop. We systematically demonstrate its capability to suppress phase noise and reduce servo bumps by adding only a single Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) controller to the loop. This class of methods is demonstrated to be conceptually concise with minimal hardware overhead, effective in practice, and holds potential for a wide variety of future applications.
items.author: Jiatian Liu, Xuan Qi, Xiayang Fan, Shenchao Jin et al.
